messages.content: Explain the kill chain methodology in penetration testing.

Lockheed Martin Cyber Kill Chain: Reconnaissance (collect target information), Weaponisation (create exploit payload), Delivery (transmit payload to target — phishing, drive-by, USB), Exploitation (trigger vulnerability — execute code on target), Installation (install backdoor for persistent access), Command & Control (C2 channel established — attacker remotely controls compromised system), Actions on Objectives (achieve goal — data exfiltration, lateral movement, ransomware). Defenders can break the kill chain at any stage — detection and response at any point prevents the final objective. Offensive teams model each stage to test whether defensive controls actually prevent progression.
What is SQL injection and how do you exploit and defend against it?

SQL injection: user-supplied input is incorporated into a database query without sanitisation, allowing the attacker to modify the query's logic. Test: input a single quote (') — if the application throws a database error, it's likely vulnerable. Exploitation: ' OR '1'='1 — always-true condition bypasses authentication. ' UNION SELECT username,password FROM users-- — extract data from other tables. Blind SQLi: no output visible but behaviour changes (Boolean-based: page changes based on true/false condition; Time-based: SLEEP() function causes delays). Full exploitation: Sqlmap automates detection, extraction, and in some cases OS command execution. Defence: parameterised queries (prepared statements) — user input never interpolated directly into SQL. WAF and input validation add layers but parameterisation is the only reliable fix.
How do you perform a web application penetration test?

Methodology (OWASP Testing Guide): (1) Information gathering — identify technologies, directories, parameters using Burp, Wappalyzer, robots.txt. (2) Authentication testing — test login for brute force protection, account enumeration, password reset flaws. (3) Session management — test for predictable tokens, insecure cookies, session fixation. (4) Input validation — test all input fields for SQLi (single quote test), XSS (alert/script tags), command injection, path traversal. (5) Access control — test whether low-privilege users can access high-privilege functions by manipulating parameters. (6) Business logic — test application-specific workflows for flaws (negative quantities, skipping steps). Document every finding with request/response evidence.
How does a professional hacking think about a target?

Adversarial mindset: assume there is always a way in. The question is never 'is this possible?' but 'what is the path of least resistance?' Process: (1) What is the highest-value asset and who has access to it? (2) What is the weakest point of entry — not the strongest? (3) What assumptions has the organisation made that might be wrong? (4) What would I do if I had 15 minutes of physical access? If I had a phishing email that got clicked? (5) Where do human factors create technical vulnerabilities? Sophisticated attackers chain together 4-5 low-severity findings that individually wouldn't be reported as critical — but together achieve total compromise. Think in chains, not in single vulnerabilities.
What is an Active Directory attack path and how do you map it?

Active Directory (AD) is the authentication/authorisation system in most corporate Windows environments. Attack paths: chains of permissions and relationships that allow movement from low-privilege to domain dominance. BloodHound: ingests AD data (via SharpHound collector) and visualises attack paths as a graph. Common paths: Kerberoasting (request service tickets for service accounts, crack offline — service accounts often have weak passwords and high privileges), Pass-the-Hash (use captured NTLM hash without knowing plaintext password), DCSync (replicate domain controller database if sufficient privileges — extracts all password hashes), Golden Ticket (forge Kerberos TGT using KRBTGT hash — persistent admin access). AD attack path reduction: least privilege, disable legacy protocols, monitor for unusual privilege use.
What is privilege escalation and how does it work?

Privilege escalation: moving from a low-privilege account to a higher-privilege one after initial access. Types: Vertical — gaining higher privileges on the same system (user → administrator/root). Horizontal — accessing another account with the same privilege level. Techniques: Exploiting SUID binaries (Linux programs that run as root regardless of who executes them), misconfigured sudo rules (sudo -l reveals what commands can be run as root), credential reuse (found credentials tried on other services), exploiting unpatched kernel vulnerabilities, DLL hijacking (Windows — replacing a DLL loaded by a privileged process), token impersonation (Windows — stealing another user's authentication token). Post-exploitation frameworks (Metasploit, Cobalt Strike) automate many of these techniques.
What is the difference between black box, white box, and grey box testing?

Black box: tester has no prior knowledge of the target — simulates an external attacker. Most realistic but least efficient. White box: tester has full knowledge — architecture diagrams, source code, credentials. Most thorough but least realistic. Grey box: partial knowledge — perhaps network diagrams or a low-privilege account. Best balance of realism and efficiency for most engagements. Methodology choice depends on objective: black box tests external attacker scenario, white box finds the most vulnerabilities in source code and architecture, grey box simulates an insider threat or attacker who has done reconnaissance.
What is penetration testing and what are its phases?

Penetration testing (pentest): authorised simulated cyberattack on a system to identify exploitable vulnerabilities before real attackers do. Phases: (1) Reconnaissance — passive (OSINT: public information about target) and active (scanning target systems). (2) Scanning & Enumeration — identify live hosts, open ports, services, software versions. (3) Vulnerability Analysis — identify weaknesses in discovered services. (4) Exploitation — attempt to exploit vulnerabilities to gain access. (5) Post-Exploitation — escalate privileges, maintain persistence, pivot to other systems, exfiltrate data. (6) Reporting — document findings with severity, evidence, and remediation guidance. All phases require written authorisation — unauthorised pentesting is illegal.
